lem-real-orthogonal-space-preliminaries:
## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space of dimension $n$, let $B$ be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form, and put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. A vector $u$ is **anisotropic** when $Q(u)\ne0$; a subspace $U$ is **totally isotropic** when $B|_{U\times U}=0$. Define $O(V,B)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}(V):B(Av,Aw)=B(v,w)\}$ and $SO(V,B)=\{A\in O(V,B):\det A=1\}$. For $U\le V$, put $U^\perp=\{v:B(v,U)=0\}$. Then:

1. $\dim U^\perp=n-\dim U$, and every totally isotropic $U$ has $\dim U\le n/2$.
2. Every such $(V,B)$ has a basis of pairwise orthogonal anisotropic vectors.
3. For $A\in O(V,B)$, $\operatorname{im}(A-I)=\ker(A-I)^\perp$.
4. For anisotropic $u$, the map $r_u(v)=v-2B(v,u)u/Q(u)$ is an orthogonal reflection: it fixes $u^\perp$, sends $u$ to $-u$, and has determinant $-1$.
lem-real-orthogonal-polar-decomposition:
## Statement

Let $p,q\ge0$, $J=\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q)$, and $A\in O(p,q)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_{p+q}(\mathbb R):A^TJA=J\}$. There are unique matrices $K$ and $P$ such that

$$A=KP,\qquad K\in O(p)\times O(q),\qquad P=(A^TA)^{1/2}>0.$$

Moreover $PJP=J$, $X=\log P$ is symmetric and satisfies $JXJ=-X$, and $K\exp(sX)\in O(p,q)$ for every real $s$. Thus $A$ is joined to its block-diagonal orthogonal factor $K$ by a path in $O(p,q)$; if $\det A=1$, the path lies in $SO(p,q)$.
lem-cartan-dieudonne-real-nondegenerate-:
## Statement

For a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $B$, every $A\in O(V,B)$ is a product of at most $\dim V$ reflections $r_u$ in anisotropic vectors $u$. The parity of the number of factors is even exactly when $A\in SO(V,B)$.
lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm:
## Statement

Let $V$ be finite-dimensional over $\mathbb R$, let $B$ be symmetric, put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and use the Clifford convention $v^2=Q(v)1$ in $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ from [[def-clifford-algebra-of-a-quadratic-space]]. The assignments $\alpha(v)=-v$ and $t(v)=v$, extended respectively as an algebra automorphism and an order-reversing anti-automorphism, descend to the quotient. Put $\bar x=t(\alpha(x))$ and $N(x)=x\bar x$. For anisotropic $u_1,\ldots,u_k$,

$$N(u_1\cdots u_k)=\prod_{j=1}^k(-Q(u_j))\,1.$$

No nondegeneracy assumption is needed for the involution and norm-of-product assertions.
def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-p:
## Definition

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space with $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ use $v^2=Q(v)1$. Use the grading involution $\alpha$ and Clifford conjugation $\bar x$ from [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Let $\mathrm{Cl}^0$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^1$ be the even and odd parts for word-length parity. Define the **unrestricted twisted Clifford normalizer** as the set

$$\Gamma(V,B)=\{x\in\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times:\alpha(x)v x^{-1}\in V\text{ for every }v\in V\},\qquad \rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)v x^{-1}.$$

Define the normalized anisotropic vectors $U(V,Q)=\{u\in V:|Q(u)|=1\}$. For $\dim V>0$, **Pin$(V,Q)$** is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times$ generated by $U(V,Q)$; for $V=0$, set Pin$(0)=\{1,-1\}$. Define

$$\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q)=\operatorname{Pin}(V,Q)\cap\mathrm{Cl}^0,\qquad \operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(V,Q)=\{x\in\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q):N(x)=1\}.$$

For definite signature, the conventional names Pin$^+(n)$ and Pin$^-(n)$ mean the groups in $\mathrm{Cl}_{n,0}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$, respectively. In mixed signature the subscript “full” is retained because the full even subgroup and the norm-one subgroup can have different images.
lem-twisted-clifford-adjoint-reflection-:
## Statement

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\Gamma$ and $\rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)vx^{-1}$ be as in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]]. For anisotropic $u$, $\rho_u=r_u$. Every $x\in\Gamma$ acts by an element of $O(V,B)$, is homogeneous, and is a nonzero scalar times a product of anisotropic vectors. The kernel of $x\mapsto\rho_x$ on $\Gamma$ is exactly $\mathbb R^\times 1$; consequently the unrestricted normalizer in the definition is a group and agrees with its homogeneous part.
lem-normalized-pin-spin-product-and-norm:
## Statement

Let $\Gamma$, Pin, $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$, $N(x)=x\bar x$, and $\rho$ have the definitions in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]] and [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Then $N$ is scalar-valued and multiplicative on $\Gamma$. For $x=u_1\cdots u_k$ with anisotropic $u_j$,

$$N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k(-Q(u_j)).$$

The subgroup generated by $|Q(u)|=1$ vectors is exactly $\{x\in\Gamma:N(x)\in\{1,-1\}\}$; it consists of normalized anisotropic-vector products, with scalar $-1$ included when $V=0$. Its even part consists of the even products and is $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$; $\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}$ is the norm-one subgroup of this full even group.
thm-real-pin-spin-image-kernel-and-compa:
## Statement

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\rho$ be the twisted action of [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]]. Then

$$1\longrightarrow\{1,-1\}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pin}(V,Q)\xrightarrow{\rho}O(V,B)\longrightarrow1$$

and

$$1\longrightarrow\{1,-1\}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q)\xrightarrow{\rho}SO(V,B)\longrightarrow1$$

are exact central group extensions. For a definite form, both groups are compact in the topology inherited from the finite-dimensional Clifford algebra. These are algebraic exactness statements; the covering-space assertion is proved separately.
lem-real-local-spin-lift-by-matrix-logar:
## Statement

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, let $J=\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n)$ be its matrix in an orthogonal anisotropic basis with $\epsilon_i=Q(e_i)\in\{1,-1\}$, and let $SO(V,B)$ have the subspace topology from matrices. There is a neighborhood $U$ of the identity in $SO(V,B)$ and a continuous map $s:U\to\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(V,Q)$ with $s(I)=1$ and $\rho(s(A))=A$.
thm-real-spin-modules-and-real-types:
## Statement

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space. The real linear span of $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q)$ inside $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ is $\mathrm{Cl}^0(V,Q)$. In particular, a subspace of a Clifford module is Spin-invariant exactly when it is a $\mathrm{Cl}^0$-submodule, and the two commutants agree. Here a **Clifford spinor representation** of full-even Spin means the restriction of a finite-dimensional unital $\mathrm{Cl}^0(V,Q)$-module. This does not mean an arbitrary group representation of Spin. Use the PA-04 even-Clifford classification in [A1] and [L1]. If

$$\mathrm{Cl}^0(V,Q)\cong\prod_{j=1}^s M_{r_j}(D_j),\qquad D_j\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\},$$

then the irreducible finite-dimensional real Clifford spinor representations are precisely one column module $D_j^{r_j}$ for each factor. Its real dimension is $r_j\dim_{\mathbb R}D_j$ and its commuting endomorphism algebra is $D_j^{\mathrm{op}}$, isomorphic to $D_j$. Distinct factors, including split factors, give inequivalent Spin modules. The module type is determined by the even algebra, not automatically by the full Clifford algebra.

In dimensions $0$ and $1$, the even Clifford algebra is $\mathbb R$ and there is one one-dimensional real Clifford spinor representation. In dimension $2$, definite signatures have even algebra $\mathbb C$ and one two-dimensional real Clifford spinor representation of complex type; signature $(1,1)$ has even algebra $\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R$ and two inequivalent one-dimensional real Clifford spinor representations.
thm-real-pin-spin-topological-double-cov:
## Statement

Equip $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ with its finite-dimensional real topology, Pin and full-even Spin with the subspace topology, and $O(V,B)$ and $SO(V,B)$ with their matrix topologies. The maps in [[thm-real-pin-spin-image-kernel-and-compactness]] are continuous central two-sheeted covering maps. This is a topological assertion in addition to the algebraic exactness of those sequences.
lem-euclidean-spin-sphere-bundle-local-s:
## Statement

Let $n\ge2$ and let $V=\mathbb R^n$ have its positive-definite inner product. Give $S^{n-1}=\{v:Q(v)=1\}$ the subspace topology and let

$$p:\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n)\to S^{n-1},\qquad p(x)=\rho_x(e_n).$$

Then $p$ is onto, the stabilizer of $e_n$ is the embedded $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n-1)$ generated by even products from $e_n^\perp$, and $p$ is a locally trivial right $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n-1)$ bundle. For unit $a$ and unit $v$ with $B(v,a)>-1$, the explicit local section is

$$s_a(v)=\frac{1+va}{\sqrt{2(1+B(v,a))}}.$$

The bundle admits a finite partition of unity whose functions have closed supports contained in the corresponding local chart domains.
thm-complex-spin-modules-and-compact-red:
## Statement

Use the complex PA-04 Clifford classification in [A1] and [A2]. For the complexification of a positive-definite real $n$-space, the irreducible Clifford spinor modules and their restrictions to full-even Spin are as follows:

- If $n=2m$ with $m\ge1$, the unique irreducible complex Clifford module has dimension $2^m$; its restriction to Spin is $S^+\oplus S^-$, with two inequivalent irreducible half-spin modules of dimension $2^{m-1}$ each.
- If $n=2m+1$, there are two inequivalent irreducible complex Clifford modules, each of dimension $2^m$; their restrictions to Spin are isomorphic to the same irreducible complex Spin module of dimension $2^m$.
- For $n=0$, there is one one-dimensional complex Clifford spinor; for $n=1$, there are two one-dimensional Clifford spinors and their restrictions to $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ agree.

Separately, assuming AC, every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of the compact Hausdorff group $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ is completely reducible. This applies to all finite-dimensional continuous representations, not only the spinor modules above.
lem-real-spin-norm-detects-components:
## Statement

Let $p,q>0$ and use signature $(+^p,-^q)$. In the polar decomposition of $A\in SO(p,q)$ from [[lem-real-orthogonal-polar-decomposition]], write $K=K_+\oplus K_-$ with $K_+\in O(p)$ and $K_-\in O(q)$. Then $\det K_+=\det K_-\in\{1,-1\}$, and

$$SO_0(p,q)=\{A\in SO(p,q):\det K_+=1\}=\rho(\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(p,q)).$$

For definite signature, $SO(p,q)$ is connected and every full-even Spin element has norm $1$, so full-even Spin and norm-one Spin have the same image and are the same subgroup. In signature $(1,1)$, the norm-one preimage of $SO_0(1,1)$ has two connected components; it is not the identity component of full-even Spin.
cor-euclidean-spin-is-universal-cover:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $n\ge3$, the connected double cover $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n)\to SO(n)$ from [[thm-real-pin-spin-topological-double-covers]] has simply connected total space and is the universal covering group of $SO(n)$. The proof uses the explicit locally trivial sphere bundle

$$\operatorname{Spin}(n-1)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spin}(n)\xrightarrow{x\mapsto\rho_x(e_n)}S^{n-1}$$

from [[lem-euclidean-spin-sphere-bundle-local-sections]]. No universal-cover assertion is made for $n=1$ or $n=2$.
